RUSSIA — Complete Country Encyclopedia

GyanBhoomi World General Knowledge | Country 002 | Research edition: 23 November 2026

Editorial note: This is a detailed reference article, not an exhaustive gazetteer of every settlement or community. It covers national systems and major regional variation. Figures are dated and attributed. Statistical estimates, census counts, legal facts and territorial claims are not interchangeable.

Territorial and statistical note: This encyclopedia uses internationally recognised country boundaries for neutral geographic description. Russia's government claims several Ukrainian territories; those claims are not recognised by the United Nations General Assembly and most states. The annexation claims are therefore described as disputed claims, not as internationally recognised Russian territory. Population and area totals from Russian domestic publications may include territories counted differently from UN statistical series. Always retain the source, reference year and territorial definition beside a number.

1.2 Name, state identity and national symbols

The name Rossiya is used in Russian for the country. The modern state is the Russian Federation, a federal republic whose constitutional text describes a multi-ethnic people and a federal structure. Its identity has been shaped by East Slavic principalities, Orthodox Christianity, steppe and Eurasian exchanges, the Russian Empire, the Soviet Union and the post-1991 federation. These layers are historically connected but are not interchangeable: the Russian state, Russian-speaking populations, ethnic Russians and the many peoples of the federation are distinct concepts.

The national flag is a horizontal white-blue-red tricolour. Its modern official status dates to the restoration of the flag in the early 1990s; historical uses of similar colours predate the present federation. The national coat of arms shows a double-headed eagle with regalia and a shield depicting a mounted figure associated with Saint George. The national anthem uses music by Alexander Alexandrov and lyrics adopted in the post-Soviet period. The anthem's history includes Soviet-era versions and changes in wording.

1.3 Constitutional and administrative identity

The Constitution adopted in 1993 establishes a federal system. It recognises different categories of federal subjects, including republics, krais, oblasts, federal cities, an autonomous oblast and autonomous okrugs. These categories have different historical and legal origins. Republics have constitutions and may establish state languages alongside Russian; other subjects generally have charters. Formal constitutional equality among subjects coexists with significant differences in population, resources, fiscal capacity and political influence.

2. Geography: a continent-sized country

2.1 Location, extent and neighbouring states

Russia extends across northern Eurasia, from the Baltic region and the borders of northern Europe to the Pacific coast. Its territory spans eleven time zones and a vast range of latitudes. The Ural Mountains are conventionally used as part of the boundary between Europe and Asia, although the exact continental boundary is a geographical convention rather than a sharp natural wall. Russia has coastlines on the Arctic and Pacific oceans and on several inland or marginal seas, including the Baltic, Black and Caspian seas.

Internationally recognised land neighbours include Norway, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania (through Kaliningrad), Poland (through Kaliningrad), Belarus, Ukraine, Georgia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, China, Mongolia and North Korea. The precise list and boundary descriptions depend on the treatment of disputed boundaries; this reference does not endorse territorial claims arising from the use of force. Maritime proximity also connects Russia to Japan and the United States across the North Pacific and Bering Strait.

2.2 Major physical regions

  1. East European Plain: a broad lowland extending west of the Urals, containing major cities, agricultural belts and river systems.
  2. Ural Mountains: a long north–south mountain chain traditionally marking part of the Europe–Asia divide and containing mineral resources.
  3. West Siberian Plain: an immense, low-lying region of wetlands, rivers, peatlands and energy resources between the Urals and Yenisei.
  4. Central Siberian Plateau: an elevated region of ancient rocks, deep river valleys and extensive taiga.
  5. Mountains of southern Siberia: Altai, Sayan and other ranges with alpine ecosystems and headwaters.
  6. Russian Far East: a complex of volcanic arcs, coastal ranges, forests, islands and active tectonic zones.
  7. North Caucasus: high mountain landscapes including the Greater Caucasus and Mount Elbrus, Europe's highest peak under the common Caucasus boundary convention.
  8. Arctic coast and islands: tundra, polar desert, permafrost, sea ice and remote archipelagos.

2.3 Mountains, volcanoes and highlands

Mount Elbrus (5,642 m) in the Caucasus is generally recognised as the highest mountain in Russia and, under the conventional Europe–Asia boundary through the Caucasus, the highest in Europe. The Altai includes Mount Belukha, while the Kamchatka Peninsula contains active volcanoes such as Klyuchevskaya Sopka. The Sikhote-Alin range in the Far East supports temperate forests and rare wildlife. The Putorana Plateau is known for basalt tablelands, deep canyons, waterfalls and lakes. Mountain environments are sensitive to warming, tourism pressure, mining and infrastructure.

2.4 Rivers and drainage basins

Russia's rivers drain to the Arctic Ocean, Pacific Ocean, Baltic and Black seas, and the Caspian basin. The Volga is Europe's longest river and is central to European Russia's transport, settlement and industrial history. The Don links the southern plain to the Sea of Azov. The Northern Dvina and Pechora flow north. In Siberia, the Ob–Irtysh, Yenisei and Lena systems are among the world's great river networks. The Amur forms part of the border with China and drains to the Pacific. River flow is strongly seasonal in many regions, with spring snowmelt floods and ice conditions shaping transport and settlement.

2.5 Lakes and inland waters

Lake Baikal in southern Siberia is the world's deepest freshwater lake and contains an exceptional share of the planet's unfrozen surface freshwater. It is also a centre of endemism, with species such as the Baikal seal. Lake Ladoga and Lake Onega are major lakes in north-western Russia. The Caspian Sea, despite its name, is the world's largest inland body of water by area and has a complex legal and ecological status. Other important water bodies include Lake Peipus on the Estonian border, the reservoirs of the Volga–Kama system and numerous Arctic and Siberian lakes.

2.6 Climate and seasons

Russia spans polar, subarctic, continental, steppe and maritime climate zones. Much of Siberia has long, severe winters and short summers. The European west is generally more maritime and less extremely cold than central and eastern Siberia. The Black Sea coast has a milder climate, while the Pacific coast is influenced by monsoonal circulation. The Arctic north experiences polar day and polar night. Seasonal snow cover, permafrost, sea ice and river freeze-up have profound effects on buildings, transport, ecosystems and livelihoods.

Climate change is particularly visible in the Arctic and sub-Arctic. Permafrost thaw can destabilise roads, pipelines and buildings; changing sea ice affects coastal communities and marine ecosystems; wildfire seasons and extreme heat have altered risks in parts of Siberia and the south. Climate impacts vary sharply by region and should be assessed using dated meteorological and scientific observations rather than generalisations.

2.7 Soils, forests and natural resources

Soils range from fertile chernozem in parts of the south to podzols, peatlands, tundra soils and permafrost-affected ground in the north and east. Russia contains the world's largest area of forest, much of it boreal taiga dominated by conifers such as larch, pine, spruce and fir. Natural resources include oil, natural gas, coal, iron ore, nickel, copper, gold, diamonds, potash, timber and hydropower potential. Resource wealth is unevenly distributed and extraction brings environmental costs, infrastructure challenges and regional dependence on commodity cycles.

2.8 Natural hazards

Hazards include earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, floods, wildfires, avalanches, landslides, severe cold, heatwaves, drought and coastal erosion. Kamchatka and the Kuril region are tectonically active. Siberian rivers can flood during snowmelt; southern regions face drought and heat; the Arctic faces coastal erosion and permafrost damage. Risk is influenced by settlement patterns, building standards, emergency services, industrial activity and changing climate conditions.

3. Population, peoples and languages

3.1 Population: estimates and census counts

UNData gives a 2025 population estimate of approximately 143.997 million, while the World Bank's 2025 series reports approximately 143.513 million. These values differ because of source series, revisions and methods. Russia's 2021 census is a national census benchmark, but census methodology and the inclusion of disputed territories are important interpretive issues. A reference article should never label a projection or estimate as a census result.

Population is unevenly distributed. The European part of the country contains most of the population and the largest urban centres. Large areas of Siberia and the Far East have very low population density because of climate, distance, terrain and infrastructure constraints. Moscow and Saint Petersburg are major metropolitan centres, while regional cities such as Novosibirsk, Yekaterinburg, Kazan, Nizhny Novgorod, Krasnoyarsk, Vladivostok and Rostov-on-Don serve as important administrative and economic hubs.

3.2 Ethnic and cultural diversity

Russia is multi-ethnic. Ethnic Russians form the largest group, but the federation includes Tatars, Bashkirs, Chechens, Chuvash, Avars, Armenians, Ukrainians, Sakha (Yakuts), Buryats, Udmurts, Mari, Mordvins, Ossetians, Kalmyks, Nenets, Evenks, Chukchi and many other peoples. Ethnicity, language, religion and citizenship are not identical categories. Individuals may identify with more than one heritage, and census responses depend on self-identification and questionnaire design.

3.3 Languages

Russian is the state language throughout the federation. The Constitution allows republics to establish their own state languages. Tatar, Bashkir, Chechen, Chuvash, Sakha, Buryat, Avar, Ossetian, Tuvan, Komi, Udmurt, Mari, Kalmyk and many other languages are used in regional, family, educational and cultural contexts. Many languages belong to Turkic, Uralic, Northeast Caucasian, Northwest Caucasian, Mongolic, Tungusic and other language families. Some Indigenous languages of the north and Far East are endangered, with speaker numbers falling and transmission to younger generations weakened.

3.4 Religion and belief

Eastern Orthodox Christianity has a major historical and institutional presence. Islam is important among Tatars, Bashkirs, peoples of the North Caucasus and other communities. Buddhism is historically rooted among Buryats, Kalmyks and Tuvans. Judaism, Armenian Christianity, Catholicism, Protestant communities, Indigenous spiritual traditions and non-religious identities are also present. Religious affiliation is diverse and should not be inferred from ethnicity or region alone. Constitutional provisions describe the state as secular and protect freedom of conscience, subject to the legal framework and its implementation.

3.5 Urbanisation, migration and demographic change

Russia is highly urbanised, with population concentrated in major cities and industrial corridors. Demographic change is shaped by fertility, mortality, life expectancy, migration, internal movement, ageing and regional inequality. Some northern and eastern regions have experienced long-term outmigration; large metropolitan areas attract students and workers. Labour migration from neighbouring countries is economically significant. Demographic data must distinguish permanent residents, temporary migrants, registered residents and people displaced by conflict.

4. History: from early Rus to the contemporary federation

4.1 Early peoples and the medieval world

The lands of present-day Russia were home to diverse hunter-gatherer, pastoralist, agricultural and trading societies long before the formation of a Russian state. Slavic communities developed across parts of eastern Europe, interacting with Finnic, Baltic, Turkic, Iranian and other peoples. The medieval polity commonly called Kievan Rus emerged around a network of towns and river routes linking the Baltic and Black Sea worlds. Kyiv was a major centre; its history belongs to the shared and contested historical narratives of modern Ukraine, Belarus and Russia. The Christianisation associated with Prince Vladimir in 988 connected the polity to Byzantine Christianity.

4.2 Mongol period and the rise of Moscow

From the thirteenth century, Mongol invasions transformed political structures across eastern Europe. Principalities paid tribute to the Golden Horde, while Moscow gradually expanded its influence. Ivan III consolidated Muscovite power in the late fifteenth century; Ivan IV was crowned tsar in 1547. Expansion eastward across Siberia accelerated from the sixteenth century, involving military conquest, trade, settlement and the incorporation of Indigenous territories. This expansion created a vast multi-ethnic empire but also produced coercion, displacement and unequal relations.

4.3 The Romanov Empire

The Romanov dynasty began in 1613 after a period of political crisis known as the Time of Troubles. Peter the Great (reigned 1682–1725) pursued military, administrative and cultural reforms, founded Saint Petersburg and expanded the empire's European orientation. Catherine II expanded territory and patronage of arts and education. Serfdom remained a defining institution until its abolition in 1861 under Alexander II. Industrialisation, railway construction, urban growth and reform developed unevenly in the nineteenth century, alongside censorship, autocracy, peasant unrest and nationalist movements.

4.4 Revolution and the Soviet Union

The First World War intensified economic and political crisis. The February Revolution of 1917 ended the monarchy; the Bolshevik Revolution in October (November in the Gregorian calendar) brought the Bolsheviks to power. Civil war and political consolidation led to the creation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics in 1922. The Soviet period included rapid industrialisation, collectivisation, famine, mass repression and the Gulag system, as well as major advances in literacy, science, public health, engineering and industrial capacity. The human cost of state violence and forced policies must be treated directly and with careful historical sourcing.

The Soviet Union played a decisive role in the Allied victory over Nazi Germany on the Eastern Front during the Second World War, known in Russia as the Great Patriotic War. The war caused enormous military and civilian losses. Post-war reconstruction, the Cold War, nuclear competition, space exploration and a centrally planned economy shaped the second half of the twentieth century. Yuri Gagarin's 1961 spaceflight became a major milestone in world history.

4.5 Perestroika, dissolution and the Russian Federation

Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms of glasnost and perestroika opened political and economic change but did not prevent the dissolution of the Soviet Union in December 1991. The Russian Federation continued the Soviet Union's UN Security Council seat. The 1990s brought market transition, privatisation, economic crisis, political conflict and the 1993 constitutional crisis. The 2000s saw stronger centralisation, commodity-led growth and expanded state capacity. Later decades included constitutional changes, sanctions, political restrictions, major conflicts and a sharp deterioration in relations with many Western states.

4.6 Russia and Ukraine: contemporary conflict and international law

Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began on 24 February 2022, following earlier conflict beginning in 2014. The invasion has caused extensive death, displacement, destruction and international consequences. The UN General Assembly has affirmed Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity and rejected attempted annexations. This encyclopedia distinguishes the Russian government's stated positions from internationally recognised borders and legal findings. It does not treat contested annexations as settled geography. Readers should consult current UN resolutions, humanitarian reporting and international law sources for developments after the research date.

5. Government, constitution and public institutions

5.1 Constitutional framework

The Constitution was adopted by referendum on 12 December 1993 and has since been amended. It defines the Russian Federation as a democratic, federal, rule-of-law state with a republican form of government. The constitutional text provides for separation of powers among the President, Federal Assembly, Government and courts. The practical operation of institutions, political competition, civil liberties and checks and balances are subjects of continuing analysis by domestic and international observers.

5.2 Federal Assembly

The Federal Assembly is the national legislature and consists of two chambers: the State Duma and the Federation Council. The State Duma is the lower chamber, with elected deputies and legislative responsibilities. The Federation Council is the upper chamber, representing federal subjects through a system defined by constitutional and federal law. Legislative procedures, election rules and membership arrangements have changed over time and should be checked against current legal texts.

5.3 President and Government

The President is head of state and holds extensive constitutional powers, including roles in foreign policy, defence, appointments and the formation of government. The Government is headed by the Prime Minister and includes federal ministers and other officials. The President appoints the Prime Minister with the State Duma's consent under the constitutional procedure. The division of powers between federal and regional institutions is shaped by constitutional provisions and federal legislation.

5.4 Judiciary and legal system

The judicial system includes the Constitutional Court, Supreme Court and courts of general and specialised jurisdiction. The Constitution guarantees judicial independence, but the independence and effectiveness of institutions in practice are assessed differently by legal scholars, human-rights organisations and international bodies. Legal summaries in this encyclopedia are educational, not legal advice. Current legislation and court decisions must be consulted for practical matters.

5.5 Federal subjects and local government

The Russian Constitution lists types of federal subjects: republics, krais, oblasts, cities of federal significance, one autonomous oblast and autonomous okrugs. The number of subjects reported by Russian official sources is affected by disputed territorial claims. For internationally neutral presentation, this encyclopedia does not reproduce the Russian government's claimed 89-subject total as an uncontested figure. A commonly used pre-2014 internationally recognised structure comprised 83 subjects; legal and administrative changes since then require careful treatment. The federal districts are administrative groupings, not constitutional subjects.

Regional government includes governors or heads of republics, legislative assemblies and local administrations. Municipal government is responsible for local services, land-use and community infrastructure under federal and regional law. The size and capacity of local government differ substantially between metropolitan centres, industrial towns, rural districts and Indigenous territories.

5.6 Elections, citizenship and rights

Russia holds presidential, parliamentary and regional elections under federal laws. Election rules, media conditions, candidate access, observation and political competition are debated by domestic and international organisations. The Constitution contains rights relating to equality, expression, assembly, religion, privacy, education and social protection. Their implementation is affected by legislation, court practice and the political environment. A balanced encyclopedia should distinguish the text of constitutional guarantees from assessments of their enforcement.

6. Economy and natural-resource systems

6.1 Economic structure

Russia has a large, resource-intensive economy with major sectors in energy, mining, manufacturing, agriculture, transport, construction, finance, retail and public services. UNData's 2025 profile reports GDP of about US$2.008 trillion in current prices and a growth estimate of 3.6% using its cited series; the World Bank's 2025 current-dollar GDP series is about US$2.56 trillion. These are not directly interchangeable without checking national-account revisions, exchange-rate conversions and source methodology. GDP measures production, not household welfare or the distribution of income.

6.2 Oil, gas and energy

Oil and natural gas have been central to exports, public revenue, industrial development and foreign relations. Major production areas include western Siberia, the Volga–Urals region, the Arctic and offshore fields. Pipelines, ports, liquefied natural gas facilities and rail infrastructure connect production to domestic and overseas markets. Coal remains important in power generation and industry. Hydropower is significant in Siberia and the Far East; nuclear power is an important part of the electricity system; wind and solar capacity are developing from a smaller base.

Energy dependence creates fiscal and geopolitical vulnerabilities. Sanctions, price caps, shipping constraints, technology restrictions, changing trade routes and investment needs have altered markets since 2022. Energy transition, methane leakage, Arctic ecosystems, oil spills and the carbon intensity of production are major environmental concerns.

6.3 Industry and manufacturing

Industrial sectors include metals, chemicals, fertilisers, machinery, automotive production, aerospace, shipbuilding, defence manufacturing, electronics, food processing and timber products. Industrial capacity is concentrated in particular regions and city clusters. Soviet-era industrial geography continues to influence factories, research institutes and transport corridors, while modern investment has changed ownership, technology and supply chains. Import substitution and domestic production policies have expanded in some sectors, but access to advanced components and international markets remains uneven.

6.4 Agriculture and food systems

Russia is a major producer and exporter of wheat and other grains. Agriculture is concentrated in the fertile southern and central black-earth zones, the Volga region, North Caucasus and selected areas of Siberia and the Far East. Crops include wheat, barley, rye, oats, sunflower, sugar beet, potatoes and vegetables. Livestock, dairy, poultry and fisheries are important. Climate variability, soil degradation, transport costs, labour availability and export policy affect agricultural outcomes.

6.5 Trade, transport and logistics

Trade routes include Baltic and Black Sea ports, Pacific ports such as Vladivostok and Nakhodka, Arctic shipping routes, rail links across Eurasia and pipelines. The Trans-Siberian Railway is a major east–west corridor. The Northern Sea Route is promoted as an Arctic shipping corridor, but seasonal ice, insurance, environmental risk, infrastructure gaps and international legal questions limit simple claims about its future. Sanctions and changing partner markets have redirected some trade flows, with effects on cost, technology access and logistics.

6.6 Currency, banking and public finance

The ruble is issued by the Bank of Russia, the central bank. Monetary policy, inflation, exchange-rate movements, banking regulation and financial sanctions shape economic conditions. Federal and regional budgets rely on taxes, transfers, commodity revenues and borrowing. Economic data should always state the year, currency basis, price basis (current or constant), and whether the value is official, estimated or forecast.

6.7 Regional inequality and economic challenges

Income and infrastructure vary between Moscow, Saint Petersburg, energy-producing regions, industrial centres, agricultural areas and remote northern or eastern settlements. Challenges include population ageing, labour shortages, regional fiscal dependence, productivity, technology access, environmental remediation, transport distances, housing quality and exposure to commodity prices. National averages can conceal significant differences in wages, public services and life expectancy.

7. Culture, arts and everyday life

7.1 Literature and language traditions

Russian literature includes medieval chronicles, religious writing, eighteenth-century poetry, nineteenth-century novels and drama, modernist movements, Soviet literature, dissident writing and contemporary fiction. Major internationally known authors include Alexander Pushkin, Mikhail Lermontov, Nikolai Gogol, Ivan Turgenev, Fyodor Dostoevsky, Leo Tolstoy, Anton Chekhov, Anna Akhmatova, Marina Tsvetaeva, Mikhail Bulgakov and many others. Literature in Tatar, Bashkir, Sakha, Buryat, Chechen and other languages forms an essential part of the country's cultural landscape.

7.2 Music, ballet and performing arts

Russian cultural history includes Orthodox chant, folk song, classical composition, opera, ballet, theatre, jazz, rock and contemporary popular music. Composers such as Tchaikovsky, Mussorgsky, Rimsky-Korsakov, Rachmaninoff, Stravinsky, Prokofiev and Shostakovich shaped international music. Ballet companies associated with the Bolshoi and Mariinsky theatres became globally influential. Regional folk instruments and traditions differ widely, from the balalaika and gusli to throat-singing traditions in Tuva and other Siberian regions.

7.3 Visual art, architecture and crafts

Architectural traditions range from medieval wooden churches and onion-domed cathedrals to Baroque and Neoclassical imperial ensembles, Constructivist architecture, Soviet monumental buildings and contemporary urban design. Icon painting, lacquer miniatures, matryoshka dolls, Gzhel ceramics, Khokhloma painting, Palekh miniatures, amber work, textiles and regional crafts have distinct histories. These crafts should not be treated as a single uniform national style.

7.4 Food and regional cuisine

Russian cuisine includes soups such as shchi and borscht (also central to Ukrainian and wider regional traditions), pelmeni, vareniki, blini, kasha, rye bread, pirozhki, pickled vegetables, fish dishes and tea culture. Tatar, Bashkir, Caucasian, Siberian, Far Eastern and northern Indigenous cuisines add distinct ingredients and methods, including dumplings, fermented foods, game, fish, berries and dairy products. Food practices vary by climate, religion, family and region; no dish represents every household.

7.5 Festivals and public celebrations

Public holidays include New Year's Day, Orthodox Christmas (7 January), Defender of the Fatherland Day, International Women's Day, Spring and Labour Day, Victory Day (9 May), Russia Day (12 June) and Unity Day (4 November). Regional calendars include Sabantuy among Tatar and Bashkir communities, Maslenitsa before Lent, Indigenous festivals, harvest celebrations and local cultural events. Observance varies by community and region.

7.6 Sport

Popular sports include football, ice hockey, figure skating, gymnastics, athletics, basketball, volleyball, wrestling, boxing, chess and biathlon. Russia and Soviet teams have had major international success in several sports. International sporting participation has been affected by governance disputes, doping sanctions and restrictions following the invasion of Ukraine; eligibility and event status change and should be verified from each sport's governing body.

8. Education, science and technology

8.1 Education system

Russia's education system includes preschool, general schooling, secondary vocational education, universities, research institutes and postgraduate training. Russian is the main language of instruction in most institutions, while some republics and minority-language communities maintain additional language education. Access and outcomes vary by region, income, urbanisation and infrastructure. International comparisons should be read with attention to assessment participation and methodology.

8.2 Universities and research institutions

Major institutions include Lomonosov Moscow State University, Saint Petersburg State University, Bauman Moscow State Technical University, Novosibirsk State University, Kazan Federal University, the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology and numerous institutes of the Russian Academy of Sciences. Research strengths have included mathematics, physics, chemistry, materials science, aerospace engineering, nuclear science, geology and Arctic studies. Institutional capacity is affected by funding, international collaboration, sanctions and researcher mobility.

8.3 Mathematics, physics and scientific traditions

Russian and Soviet scientists made major contributions to mathematics, theoretical physics, chemistry, engineering and computing. Figures include Mikhail Lomonosov, Dmitri Mendeleev, Sofia Kovalevskaya, Nikolai Lobachevsky, Andrey Kolmogorov, Lev Landau, Igor Tamm, Pyotr Kapitsa and many others. Scientific achievements emerged from international exchange as well as domestic institutions; they should not be framed as isolated national inventions.

8.4 Space exploration

The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 in 1957, the first artificial satellite, and sent Yuri Gagarin into space in 1961, the first human spaceflight. Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in 1963. The Soviet programme developed lunar and planetary probes, long-duration spaceflight, space stations and launch systems. The Russian Federation inherited major elements of the Soviet space infrastructure and participates in human spaceflight and satellite programmes. The International Space Station has been a major international collaboration. Current programme schedules, launch statistics and partnerships must be checked against Roscosmos and partner agencies.

8.5 Nuclear, aviation and engineering

Russia has a major nuclear energy and nuclear engineering sector, including reactor design, fuel services and nuclear research. Aviation and aerospace manufacturing includes civilian and military aircraft, helicopters, engines and launch vehicles. Engineering expertise is also found in rail transport, metallurgy, hydropower, Arctic infrastructure and heavy industry. Technology transfer constraints and supply-chain disruptions have affected several sectors since 2022.

8.6 Digital systems and contemporary innovation

Digital services, software, cybersecurity, telecommunications, artificial intelligence, financial technology and e-government have developed in major cities. The digital economy is shaped by domestic platforms, regulation, data-localisation requirements and restricted access to some international technology markets. Claims about technological independence or capability should be supported by measurable production, deployment and research evidence.

9. Tourism, heritage and natural wonders

9.1 UNESCO World Heritage

UNESCO's Russian Federation country page lists 33 World Heritage properties in the currently consulted register: 22 cultural, 11 natural and 0 mixed. Examples include the Historic Centre of Saint Petersburg and Related Groups of Monuments; Kremlin and Red Square, Moscow; Kizhi Pogost; Lake Baikal; Volcanoes of Kamchatka; Golden Mountains of Altai; Western Caucasus; Virgin Komi Forests; Lena Pillars; and the Landscapes of Dauria. The UNESCO list is live and should be checked before publication because inscriptions, conservation status and site boundaries can change.

9.2 Historic cities and architectural destinations

Moscow contains the Kremlin, Red Square, Saint Basil's Cathedral, the Bolshoi Theatre and major museums. Saint Petersburg is known for the Hermitage, Peterhof, the historic centre, canals and imperial architecture. The Golden Ring includes historic towns such as Vladimir, Suzdal, Yaroslavl, Rostov Veliky and Sergiev Posad. Kazan combines Tatar and Russian histories; Veliky Novgorod preserves major medieval monuments; Kaliningrad has a distinct Baltic and Prussian heritage; Vladivostok is a Pacific port city.

9.3 Natural attractions

  • Lake Baikal and its surrounding mountains.
  • Volcanoes and geysers of Kamchatka.
  • Altai mountains, glaciers and alpine lakes.
  • Putorana Plateau and its waterfalls.
  • Curonian Spit dunes and coastal forests.
  • Virgin Komi Forests and northern taiga.
  • Western Caucasus and Mount Elbrus.
  • Lena Pillars along the Lena River.
  • Wrangel Island Arctic landscapes.
  • Russian Far East forests and Sikhote-Alin biodiversity.

9.4 Responsible travel and access

Travel conditions, visa rules, insurance, transport routes, payment systems, border access and safety advisories can change rapidly. Sanctions and international restrictions may affect flights, banking, connectivity and consular support. Visitors should consult their own government's current travel advice and official Russian entry requirements. Protected areas may require permits, guides or seasonal access. Respect for Indigenous communities, wildlife and fragile ecosystems is essential.

10. International relations and contemporary affairs

10.1 International organisations

Russia is a permanent member of the UN Security Council and participates in organisations and forums including the G20, BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, the Commonwealth of Independent States, the Eurasian Economic Union, the Collective Security Treaty Organization and the Arctic Council (whose work has been disrupted by geopolitical tensions). Membership, participation and suspension status vary by institution and date.

10.2 Foreign policy themes

Foreign policy has involved security concerns, energy exports, arms sales, relations with neighbouring states, the Arctic, Eurasian integration and a stated preference for a multipolar international order. Relations with the European Union, United States and many other states deteriorated sharply following the 2014 annexation of Crimea and the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Other states maintain different approaches, including sanctions, diplomatic engagement, neutrality or expanded trade. A reference work should describe these positions with dated evidence rather than treating geopolitical narratives as settled fact.

10.3 The Arctic

Russia has the longest Arctic coastline and extensive Arctic infrastructure, including settlements, ports, research stations and energy projects. The region is strategically important for shipping, resources, military security and climate science. Melting sea ice may lengthen some navigation windows but does not remove severe weather, darkness, remoteness, ecological sensitivity or legal questions. Indigenous peoples of the Arctic have rights, livelihoods and knowledge systems that must be included in policy and environmental discussions.

11. Environment, biodiversity and conservation

11.1 Ecosystems and biomes

Russia contains Arctic tundra, boreal taiga, temperate forests, steppe, semi-desert, mountain ecosystems, wetlands, freshwater systems and Pacific coastal habitats. The taiga stores large quantities of carbon and supports species adapted to long winters. Permafrost landscapes are globally important for climate science. The Far East has a mixture of temperate and subtropical influences, including forests with high biodiversity.

11.2 Iconic wildlife

Species include the Amur tiger, Amur leopard, brown bear, polar bear, Eurasian lynx, wolf, wolverine, reindeer, saiga antelope, Siberian crane, snow leopard, musk deer, sable, Arctic fox, Baikal seal and numerous salmon species. Habitat loss, poaching, infrastructure, climate change, pollution and human-wildlife conflict affect conservation. The Amur leopard remains critically endangered; the exact status of species should be checked against the IUCN Red List and national monitoring programmes.

11.3 Protected areas and conservation

Protected-area categories include zapovedniks (strict nature reserves), national parks, wildlife refuges and regional protected areas. The system includes places such as Barguzinsky, Kronotsky, Sikhote-Alin, Stolby, Sochi, the Commander Islands and many others. Protected-area status, boundaries and management rules differ; a complete current register should be sourced from the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment and official regional agencies.

11.4 Environmental pressures

Pressures include oil and gas extraction, mining, industrial pollution, forest fires, illegal logging, overfishing, waste management, urban air pollution, river contamination, permafrost thaw and habitat fragmentation. Lake Baikal faces pressures from wastewater, tourism, shoreline development and climate-related ecological change. Environmental outcomes vary by region and require transparent monitoring.

12. Transport, infrastructure and communications

12.1 Railways

The Trans-Siberian Railway connects Moscow with Vladivostok across a route of roughly 9,289 kilometres, depending on route definition. It is a major passenger and freight corridor and a symbol of the integration of Siberia and the Far East. Other important routes include the Baikal–Amur Mainline (BAM), regional railways and metro systems in major cities. Rail infrastructure is essential because distances are vast and some settlements are not connected by all-season roads.

12.2 Roads, aviation and shipping

Road networks are densest in European Russia and major southern corridors. In remote regions, winter roads, river transport and seasonal routes remain important. Aviation connects distant cities and northern settlements. Major ports include Saint Petersburg, Novorossiysk, Murmansk, Vladivostok, Nakhodka and others. Arctic shipping is constrained by ice, weather, infrastructure, environmental protection and geopolitics.

12.3 Cities and urban infrastructure

Moscow and Saint Petersburg have extensive metro and suburban rail systems. Other cities have trams, trolleybuses, buses and developing metro or rapid transit networks. Urban challenges include housing quality, ageing infrastructure, air pollution, traffic, heating systems, public space and unequal access to services. Soviet-era urban planning remains visible in many cities, alongside contemporary development.

13. Health, society and quality of life

Russia's health system combines federal and regional public services with private providers. Important public-health issues include cardiovascular disease, cancer, alcohol-related harm, tobacco use, infectious disease, mental health, rural access, ageing and regional differences in life expectancy. The World Bank reports life expectancy at birth of about 73 years in 2024 in its current series. This is a national aggregate and masks substantial differences by sex, region and socioeconomic status.

Social policy includes pensions, education, family support, housing, public health and regional transfers. The lived experience of residents differs by income, urban/rural location, ethnicity, disability, gender, age and access to services. Social indicators should be compared using consistent definitions and year-specific sources.

14. Important records, achievements and global significance

  • Russia is the world's largest country by surface area in widely used UN statistical series.
  • It spans eleven time zones.
  • Lake Baikal is the world's deepest freshwater lake.
  • The Volga is Europe's longest river.
  • Mount Elbrus is commonly recognised as Europe's highest mountain under the Caucasus boundary convention.
  • Sputnik 1, launched in 1957 by the Soviet Union, was the first artificial satellite.
  • Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space in 1961.
  • Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in 1963.
  • The Trans-Siberian Railway is one of the world's longest continuous rail routes.
  • Russia has extensive Arctic territory and coastline.
  • Russian literature, music, ballet, mathematics and scientific traditions have had global influence.
  • Russia is a permanent member of the UN Security Council.

Record claims depend on definitions, geographic conventions and date. The largest country by area, deepest lake, longest railway and first spaceflight are useful facts only when the relevant measurement or historical definition is stated.

16. Country quiz — 30 questions with answers and explanations

Q1. What is the official name of Russia?
Answer: Russian Federation.
Explanation: This is the constitutional name of the federal state.

Q2. What is the capital city?
Answer: Moscow.
Explanation: Moscow is the national capital and largest metropolitan centre.

Q3. Which mountain range is often used as the Europe–Asia boundary?
Answer: The Ural Mountains.
Explanation: This is a conventional geographic boundary, not a political border.

Q4. What is Russia's currency?
Answer: Russian ruble.
Explanation: Its ISO currency code is RUB.

Q5. How many time zones does Russia use?
Answer: Eleven.
Explanation: The zones range from UTC+2 to UTC+12.

Q6. Which is Europe's longest river?
Answer: The Volga.
Explanation: It flows through western Russia to the Caspian Sea.

Q7. Which is the world's deepest freshwater lake?
Answer: Lake Baikal.
Explanation: It is in southern Siberia and has exceptional biodiversity.

Q8. What is Mount Elbrus's elevation?
Answer: 5,642 metres.
Explanation: It is in the Caucasus and is commonly considered Europe's highest mountain.

Q9. Which city was founded by Peter the Great in 1703?
Answer: Saint Petersburg.
Explanation: It became an imperial capital and a major Baltic port.

Q10. When did the Romanov dynasty begin?
Answer: 1613.
Explanation: It followed the Time of Troubles.

Q11. When was serfdom abolished in the Russian Empire?
Answer: 1861.
Explanation: The reform was enacted under Alexander II.

Q12. In which year did the Russian revolutions take place?
Answer: 1917.
Explanation: The February Revolution ended the monarchy; the Bolshevik Revolution followed later that year.

Q13. When was the Soviet Union established?
Answer: 1922.
Explanation: The USSR was formed as a union of Soviet republics.

Q14. When did the Soviet Union dissolve?
Answer: 1991.
Explanation: The Russian Federation emerged as the principal successor state.

Q15. What was Sputnik 1?
Answer: The first artificial satellite, launched in 1957 by the Soviet Union.
Explanation: It marked the beginning of the space age.

Q16. Who was the first human in space?
Answer: Yuri Gagarin.
Explanation: He orbited Earth in Vostok 1 in April 1961.

Q17. Who was the first woman in space?
Answer: Valentina Tereshkova.
Explanation: She flew aboard Vostok 6 in 1963.

Q18. Which railway links Moscow and Vladivostok?
Answer: The Trans-Siberian Railway.
Explanation: It is a major east–west transport corridor.

Q19. Which peninsula is famous for volcanoes and geysers?
Answer: Kamchatka.
Explanation: It lies in the Russian Far East along an active tectonic zone.

Q20. Which city is home to the Hermitage Museum?
Answer: Saint Petersburg.
Explanation: The museum is housed in the Winter Palace complex and associated buildings.

Q21. What is the lower chamber of the Federal Assembly?
Answer: State Duma.
Explanation: It is the lower house of the national legislature.

Q22. What is the upper chamber called?
Answer: Federation Council.
Explanation: It represents federal subjects through constitutional arrangements.

Q23. What is the federal state language?
Answer: Russian.
Explanation: Republics may also establish their own state languages.

Q24. Which large inland water body borders Russia to the south?
Answer: The Caspian Sea.
Explanation: It is the world's largest inland water body by area.

Q25. Which species is strongly associated with the Russian Far East?
Answer: Amur tiger.
Explanation: Its remaining wild population is concentrated in the Russian Far East and adjacent areas.

Q26. Which city is a major centre of Tatar culture?
Answer: Kazan.
Explanation: It is the capital of the Republic of Tatarstan.

Q27. What is Russia's national day?
Answer: Russia Day, 12 June.
Explanation: It commemorates the 1990 declaration of state sovereignty.

Q28. How many UNESCO World Heritage properties are listed on the consulted Russia page?
Answer: 33.
Explanation: UNESCO's live country page lists 22 cultural and 11 natural properties; check for updates.

Q29. When did Russia launch its full-scale invasion of Ukraine?
Answer: 24 February 2022.
Explanation: The invasion escalated a conflict that had begun in 2014.

Q30. Are Russia's claims to annex Ukrainian territories internationally recognised?
Answer: No.
Explanation: The UN General Assembly has rejected the attempted annexations and affirmed Ukraine's territorial integrity.

17. Glossary of essential terms

  • Federation: a state in which constitutional powers are divided between national and regional governments.
  • Federal subject: a constituent unit of the Russian Federation.
  • Oblast: a type of federal subject broadly comparable to a region or province.
  • Krai: a type of federal subject with historical roots in frontier or territory administration.
  • Republic: a federal subject with its own constitution and the ability to establish state languages.
  • Autonomous okrug: a federal subject historically associated with particular Indigenous or national communities.
  • Taiga: northern boreal forest biome.
  • Tundra: cold biome with low vegetation, short growing season and often permafrost.
  • Permafrost: ground that remains at or below 0°C for at least two consecutive years.
  • Steppe: temperate grassland with limited tree cover.
  • Zapovednik: strict nature reserve in the Russian protected-area system.
  • Perestroika: restructuring reforms introduced during the late Soviet period.
  • Glasnost: openness and increased public discussion during Gorbachev's reforms.
  • Ruble: Russian currency unit, divided into 100 kopeks.
  • Trans-Siberian Railway: major rail route connecting European Russia with the Pacific coast.
  • Arctic Council: intergovernmental forum for Arctic states and Indigenous participants.
  • UNESCO World Heritage: international designation for cultural or natural properties of outstanding universal value.

Federal-subject category explainer

The Constitution distinguishes republics, krais, oblasts, federal cities, an autonomous oblast and autonomous okrugs. A list of names and counts must be dated and must state its territorial definition. Since Russia's claims over Ukrainian territories are not recognised by the UN General Assembly, this encyclopedia does not present a claimed 89-subject list as an internationally accepted administrative map. For legal and current domestic administration, consult the Russian Constitution and official registers, then compare with UN-recognised boundaries and international law sources.

22. Annexure E — Source register and update policy

Core statistical and institutional sources

  1. UNData — Russian Federation: data.un.org/legacy/en/iso/ru.html — population, area, capital, currency and economic series.
  2. World Bank — Russian Federation: data.worldbank.org/country/russian-federation — population, GDP, life expectancy and development indicators.
  3. Rosstat: eng.rosstat.gov.ru — Russian official statistics; interpret territorial coverage and methodology.
  4. UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Russian Federation: whc.unesco.org/en/statesparties/RU/ — current property register.
  5. Constitution of the Russian Federation: Refworld text — federal structure and constitutional provisions.
  6. UN General Assembly resolutions: un.org/en/ga — resolutions on Ukraine's territorial integrity and attempted annexations.
  7. UNHCR Ukraine situation: data.unhcr.org/en/situations/ukraine — displacement and humanitarian context.
  8. NASA History: nasa.gov/history — space history and international milestones.
  9. Roscosmos: roscosmos.ru — official Russian space programme information.
  10. Arctic Council: arctic-council.org — Arctic cooperation, environment and Indigenous participation.
  11. IUCN Red List: iucnredlist.org — species status and conservation assessment.
  12. Convention on Biological Diversity: cbd.int — biodiversity and national reporting.

Editorial and update policy

  • Population: update from UN World Population Prospects and World Bank; preserve the estimate year and distinguish from census.
  • Area and territorial boundaries: state the geographic definition; distinguish internationally recognised borders from claims not recognised by the UN General Assembly.
  • Federal subjects: update legal changes and clearly state the territorial coverage used.
  • GDP and trade: specify current or constant prices, currency, conversion method and reference year.
  • Current officeholders and political developments: verify on publication day and show the verification date.
  • UNESCO properties: use the live UNESCO register and update after each World Heritage Committee session.
  • Wildlife: verify threatened status against IUCN and national scientific sources.
  • Climate: use dated observations and peer-reviewed assessments; distinguish observed trends from projections.
  • Maps: use neutral, internationally recognised boundaries and label disputed territories clearly; never depict annexation claims as settled international borders.
  • Photographs: preserve the source page, creator, licence and attribution; remove images with unclear rights or misleading captions.
